craft_claim: Indian poetics theorises the grim register as karuna (grief/compassion) and bhayanaka (terror), relished as rasa when suggested (dhvani) rather than stated, so bleakness need not be affectless to be art.

supporting_evidence.note: Bharata's taxonomy enumerates karuna (the pathetic/grief-laden) and bhayanaka (the terrible/fearful) among the rasas, alongside vibhatsa (the odious); no meaning is held to proceed without rasa.

supporting_evidence.location: Uddyota 1 (dhvani as the soul of poetry)
supporting_evidence.note: Anandavardhana holds that suggested meaning (dhvani) outranks literal statement; in the grim register, sorrow and dread land hardest when evoked rather than announced.
Tendulkar's political tragedy stages caste violence and instrumentality without redemption, working through karuna and a chorus that frames rather than consoles.

counterevidence.note: Section E translation limit: karuna and bhayanaka do not map one-to-one onto 'grief' and 'horror' in Ghosh's rendering, so the mapping of the rasas onto a modern grim register is analogical and translation-mediated.

scope: Indian dramatic and poetic traditions; transferable to any tradition that distinguishes evoked from stated emotion.
exceptions: Classical rasa is a spectator-relished aesthetic emotion; it is not identical to modern realist 'grit', and the mapping is analogical.
